content.text:
I submitted **factor-when-justified** with confidence 0.8. I used 47 of the 60 budget.

**Round 1.** I trained 3 tasks so that each rule appeared exactly once: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3.
- L3-S1-M2 reuses three rules the learner had already seen, and its similarity to the training set was 0.375. It took 47 and 55 examples.
- L4-S4-M2 has two rules the learner had never seen, but its similarity was 0.625. It took 32 and 19 examples.

The task with more new rules was cheaper, which points to a learner driven by similarity rather than a part-based one. With only two tests each, this was weak evidence on its own.

**Round 2.** I trained 6 more tasks so that L3, S1 and M2 each appeared in 3 trained tasks. I chose them so that L3-S1-M2's highest similarity to the training set stayed at 0.375.
- **L3-S1-M2:** it fell to an average of 23.8 examples over 13 tests.
- **L1-S4-M4 (control):** its highest similarity is also 0.375, but each of its rules had been trained only once. It averaged 43.3 over 14 tests.
- **L1-S3-M4:** one of its rules had been trained twice. It came in between at 30.1 over 7 tests.

The gap between the main task and the control is about 3 standard errors.

**Why this picks factor-when-justified:**
- **Holistic** predicts the main task and the control cost the same, because their similarity is matched.
- **Part-based** also predicts they cost the same, because by round 2 the learner had seen every rule in both tasks.
- **Factor-when-justified** is the only hypothesis that predicts the main task gets cheaper once each of its rules has been trained 3 times.

**Caveats:**
- Single test results varied enormously; the same task gave anywhere from 1 to 53.
- The comparison only matched the highest similarity. If the learner also weighs similarity to its other trained tasks, that isn't controlled, though the control's average similarity was if anything slightly higher.
- I can't tell whether the threshold k is 2 or 3.
